ch49.title: Golgotha
ch49.b001: Friday Morning: John Goes to Bethany
ch49.b002: As Jesus and his accusers started off to see Herod, the Master turned to the Apostle John, who was still at his side, and made a last request of him. “⟦Q 186:0.1⟧John, you can do no more for me. Go to my mother and bring her to see me ere I die.⟦/Q⟧” John was reluctant to leave his Master alone among his enemies, but he did as he was asked and hastened off over the hill to Bethany. There, at the home of Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus whom Jesus had raised from the dead, the entire family of Jesus was assembled in waiting. Several times during the morning messengers had brought news of the trial to the house, yet the family themselves had reached Bethany only a few minutes before John came through the door bearing the Master’s request that his mother come to him before he was put to death.
ch49.b003: John told them all that had happened since the midnight arrest. Mary the mother of Jesus went at once in his company to see her eldest son. His sister Ruth refused to remain behind with the others, and since she was determined to go with her mother, her brother Jude went with her. The rest of the family stayed in Bethany under the direction of James, and almost every hour the messengers of David Zebedee came to the door with reports of that terrible business of putting to death their eldest brother, Jesus of Nazareth. But by the time Mary and John reached Jerusalem, Jesus, accompanied by the Roman soldiers who were to crucify him, had already arrived at Golgotha.
ch49.b005: It was about half past eight that Friday morning when the hearing before Pilate ended and the Master was placed in the custody of the Roman soldiers. The captain of the Jewish guards marched his men back to their temple headquarters, and Caiaphas and his Sanhedrist associates followed close behind, going directly to their usual meeting place in the hall of hewn stone. Many other members of the Sanhedrin were waiting there to learn what had been done with Jesus. As Caiaphas was making his report, Judas appeared to claim his reward. All these men loathed him. Though pricked in his conscience and already somewhat disillusioned, he still expected to be called before the full council, to hear himself eulogized, and to receive suitable honors for the great service he flattered himself he had rendered his nation. Instead, a servant of the high priest tapped him on the shoulder, called him just outside the hall, and said: “⟦Q 186:1.2⟧Judas, I have been appointed to pay you for the betrayal of Jesus. Here is your reward.⟦/Q⟧” He handed him a bag containing thirty pieces of silver—the current price of a good, healthy slave.
ch49.b006: Judas was stunned, dumfounded. He rushed back to enter the hall, but the doorkeeper barred his way. He could not believe that the rulers of the Jews would allow him to betray his friends and his Master and then offer him thirty pieces of silver. Humiliated and utterly crushed, he walked away from the temple as if in a trance. Automatically he dropped the money bag into his deep pocket, the same pocket wherein he had so long carried the apostolic funds, and he wandered out through the city after the crowds who were on their way to witness the crucifixions. From a distance he saw them raise the crossbeam with Jesus nailed thereon. At that sight he rushed back to the temple, forced his way past the doorkeeper, and found himself standing before the Sanhedrin, still in session. Well-nigh breathless and highly distraught, he managed to stammer out: “⟦Q 186:1.4⟧I have sinned in that I have betrayed innocent blood. You have insulted me. You have offered me as a reward for my service, money—the price of a slave. I repent that I have done this; here is your money. I want to escape the guilt of this deed.⟦/Q⟧”
ch49.b007: The rulers scoffed at him. One of them, sitting near where Judas stood, motioned that he should leave and said: “⟦Q 186:1.5⟧Your Master has already been put to death by the Romans, and as for your guilt, what is that to us? See you to that—and begone!⟦/Q⟧” As he left the chamber, Judas took the thirty pieces of silver from the bag and threw them broadcast over the temple floor. All the glamor, fascination, and intoxication of wrongdoing had vanished. Now the evildoer stood alone, face to face with the judgment verdict of his disillusioned and disappointed soul. This onetime ambassador of the kingdom of heaven walked through the streets of Jerusalem forsaken and alone, out through the walls and down into the terrible solitude of the valley of Hinnom. There he climbed the steep rocks, fastened one end of the girdle of his cloak to a small tree, tied the other about his neck, and cast himself over the precipice. Ere he was dead, the knot which his nervous hands had tied gave way, and his body was dashed to pieces on the jagged rocks below.
ch49.b009: Shortly after Jesus was handed over to the Romans, a detachment of the temple guards hastened out to Gethsemane to disperse or arrest the Master’s followers. But they had long since scattered. The apostles had retired to designated hiding places, the Greeks had gone to various homes in Jerusalem, and the other disciples had likewise disappeared. David Zebedee, believing that the enemies would return, had early removed five or six tents up the ravine near the spot where the Master so often went to pray, and there he kept a hidden center for his messenger service. He had hardly left the camp when the guards arrived. Finding no one, they contented themselves with burning the camp and hurried back to the temple. On hearing their report, the Sanhedrin was satisfied that the followers of Jesus were too frightened to attempt an uprising or a rescue. At last able to breathe easily, they adjourned, every man going his way to prepare for the Passover.
ch49.b010: As soon as Pilate had turned Jesus over for crucifixion, a messenger ran to Gethsemane to inform David, and within five minutes runners were on their way to Bethsaida, Pella, Philadelphia, Sidon, Shechem, Hebron, Damascus, and Alexandria. Throughout that tragic day David sent messengers about every half hour to the apostles, the Greeks, and Jesus’ family at Bethany. This peculiar-minded man was the only one of the leading disciples who took a literal, matter-of-fact view of the Master’s assertion that he would die and “⟦Q 186:3.4⟧rise again on the third day.⟦/Q⟧” He had once heard him say it, and he quietly proposed to assemble all his messengers early Sunday morning at the home of Nicodemus, so that they would be on hand to spread the news in case Jesus rose from the dead. Finding that no one else expected such a thing so soon, he said little about his belief.
ch49.b012: It was a little after eight o’clock when Pilate washed his hands before the multitude and gave the word that Jesus was to be crucified immediately. The soldiers led him back into the courtyard of the praetorium, took off the robe Herod had put on him, and dressed him in his own garments. They mocked and derided him, but they inflicted no further punishment. Jesus was now alone with these Roman soldiers. His friends were in hiding, his enemies had gone their way, and even John was no longer by his side. During more than half an hour of waiting he never spoke a word, and the soldiers began to be impressed by his unusual composure, his extraordinary dignity, his uncomplaining silence. Much of the delay was due to the captain’s last-minute decision to take along two thieves already condemned to die. They were associates of Barabbas and would later have been put to death with their leader had he not been released as the Passover pardon. Jesus was thus crucified in the place of Barabbas.
ch49.b013: There is no direct relation between the death of Jesus and the Jewish Passover, though he died on the day of preparation, at about the time the Passover lambs were being sacrificed in the temple. It was man and not God who planned and executed his death on the cross. The Father refused to interfere with the march of human events, but he did not decree, demand, or require the death of his Son. Jesus went to it of his own free will, as he had once foretold: “⟦Q 187:0.3⟧No one takes my life away from me—I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up. I have received such a commandment from my Father.⟦/Q⟧”
ch49.b014: Just before nine o’clock the procession left the praetorium. Jesus bore the crossbeam on his shoulders; the upright timbers had already been planted in the ground at Golgotha. The centurion led the way carrying the small white boards. The notice for Jesus had been written by Pilate himself in Latin, Greek, and Aramaic: “⟦Q 187:1.2⟧Jesus of Nazareth—the King of the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” Some of the Jewish authorities had protested and pleaded that it at least read, “⟦Q 187:1.3⟧He said, ‘I am the king of the Jews,’⟦/Q⟧” but Pilate only replied, “⟦Q 187:1.3⟧What I have written, I have written.⟦/Q⟧” Some two hundred or more followed, most of them enemies or curious idlers, along the most direct way to the Damascus gate on the north.
ch49.b015: As the procession passed through the narrow streets, many tenderhearted women who had heard his words of good cheer could not refrain from weeping, though it was strictly against the law to show sympathy for one being led to crucifixion. When some even dared to walk beside him, the Master turned his head toward them and said: “⟦Q 187:1.6⟧Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but rather weep for yourselves and for your children. My work is about done—soon I go to my Father—but the times of terrible trouble for Jerusalem are just beginning.⟦/Q⟧” He had had neither food nor water since the Last Supper, nor one moment of sleep. Shortly after passing through the gate he fell beneath the weight of the crossbeam. The soldiers shouted and kicked him, but he could not rise. The captain, knowing what Jesus had already endured, commanded them to desist and compelled a passerby, one Simon from Cyrene, to carry the beam the rest of the way. After the resurrection this Passover pilgrim from northern Africa became a valiant believer, and his two sons, Alexander and Rufus, became effective teachers of the gospel in Africa. Yet he never knew that the man whose burden he bore was the same Jewish tutor who had once befriended his injured son.
ch49.b017: It was shortly after nine when the procession of death reached Golgotha. The soldiers bound the Master’s arms with cords to the crossbeam and nailed his hands to the wood. When they had hoisted the beam up on the post and fastened it, they nailed his feet with one long nail through both. The cross was not high; his feet were only about three feet from the ground, so that he could hear every taunt and see plainly the faces of those who mocked him. A society of Jewish women always sent someone to offer drugged wine to the crucified, but when Jesus tasted it, thirsty as he was, he refused to drink. He chose to retain his human consciousness until the very end and to meet death by voluntary submission to the full human experience.
ch49.b018: The two brigands had been put on their crosses first, cursing and spitting on their executioners. Jesus’ only words, as they nailed him to the crossbeam, were, “⟦Q 187:2.4⟧Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.⟦/Q⟧” Then the captain nailed the title above his head. Just at that moment John arrived with Mary the mother of Jesus, Ruth, and Jude. As Jesus saw his mother, with John and his brother and sister, he smiled but said nothing. Below him the four soldiers divided his clothes as was the custom, one taking the sandals, one the turban, one the girdle, and the fourth the cloak. The seamless tunic was too unusual to cut into pieces, so they cast lots for it. It was well that the soldiers took his clothing, for the Master desired that his followers should have nothing material to associate with his life on earth. He wished to leave mankind only the memory of a human life consecrated to doing the Father’s will.
ch49.b019: By eleven o’clock upward of a thousand persons had gathered, while the unseen hosts of a universe stood in silence, gazing upon the Creator dying the death of a condemned criminal. Many who passed by wagged their heads and railed: “⟦Q 187:3.3⟧You who would destroy the temple and build it again in three days, save yourself.⟦/Q⟧” Some of the rulers mocked, “⟦Q 187:3.3⟧He saved others, but himself he cannot save.⟦/Q⟧” But since Jesus made no reply, and noontime of the preparation day drew near, by half past eleven fewer than fifty persons remained. The soldiers settled down to eat their lunch and drink their cheap, sour wine, and they derisively offered a toast: “⟦Q 187:3.4⟧Hail and good fortune! to the king of the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” Looking down on them, he said, “I thirst.” The captain of the guard put the wine-soaked sponge stopper of his bottle on the end of a javelin and raised it so that Jesus could moisten his parched lips. He had lived as a man, and he would die as a man—doing the Father’s will.
ch49.b021: One of the brigands railed at him: “⟦Q 187:4.1⟧If you are the Son of God, why do you not save yourself and us?⟦/Q⟧” But the other, who had many times heard the Master teach, both in the temple and months before at the Pella camp, answered: “⟦Q 187:4.1⟧Do you have no fear even of God? Do you not see that we are suffering justly for our deeds, but that this man suffers unjustly? Better that we should seek forgiveness for our sins and salvation for our souls.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus turned his face toward him and smiled approvingly. Seeing that face, the malefactor mustered his courage, fanned the flickering flame of his faith, and said, “⟦Q 187:4.1⟧Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus said, “⟦Q 187:4.1⟧Verily, verily, I say to you today, you shall sometime be with me in Paradise.⟦/Q⟧”
ch49.b022: This young man had been led into violence by those who praised robbery as a patriotic protest against oppression, and he had looked upon Barabbas as a hero. Now, on the cross beside him, he saw a true hero, one who quickened all his ideals of courage and moral self-respect. Had any other person in the jeering crowd experienced the birth of faith in his soul and appealed to the mercy of Jesus, he would have been received with the same loving consideration. John was away in the city at the time, and Luke later heard the story from the converted Roman captain of the guard.
ch49.b023: Noon: The Mother and the Disciple
ch49.b024: Just after the thief had heard the Master’s promise, John returned from the city, bringing his mother, Salome, and almost a dozen women believers. He took his place near Mary the mother of Jesus, supporting her, while her son Jude stood on the other side. It was noontide. Jesus looked down upon them and said to his mother, “Woman, behold your son!” And speaking to John, he said, “My son, behold your mother!” Then he addressed them both: “⟦Q 187:4.7⟧I desire that you depart from this place.⟦/Q⟧” And so John and Jude led Mary away from Golgotha. John took her to the place where he tarried in Jerusalem and then hastened back. After the Passover Mary returned to Bethsaida, where she lived at John’s home for the rest of her life; she did not live quite one year after the death of Jesus. The other women withdrew a short distance and remained there until the end.
ch49.b025: The Last Hour in the Sandstorm
ch49.b026: Shortly after twelve o’clock, though it was early in the season for it, the sky darkened with fine sand in the air, the sign of a hot-wind sandstorm from the Arabian Desert. Before one o’clock the sun was hidden, and the rest of the crowd hastened back to the city. Shortly after one, amid the deepening darkness, Jesus began to fail in human consciousness. His mind turned to passages he knew by heart, especially the twentieth, twenty-first, and twenty-second Psalms. His lips often moved, but he was too weak to utter the words; only a few times did those standing by catch something: “⟦Q 187:5.2⟧I know the Lord will save his anointed,⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 187:5.2⟧Your hand shall find out all my enemies,⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 187:5.2⟧My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?⟦/Q⟧” He did not feel that the Father had forsaken him. He never doubted that he was laying down his life in accordance with his Father’s will; he was merely reciting, in his vanishing consciousness, the psalm that begins with those words.
ch49.b027: About half past one he said a second time, “I thirst,” and the same captain moistened his lips with the sponge wet in the sour wine then commonly called vinegar. The sandstorm grew fiercer and the heavens darker. The soldiers crouched together near the cross against the cutting sand, while Salome and others watched from the shelter of an overhanging rock. When the end came, there stood at the foot of the cross John Zebedee, Jesus’ brother Jude, his sister Ruth, Mary Magdalene, and Rebecca, onetime of Sepphoris.
ch49.b028: It was just before three o’clock when Jesus, with a loud voice, cried out, “⟦Q 187:5.5⟧It is finished! Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.⟦/Q⟧” And when he had thus spoken, he bowed his head and gave up the life struggle. The Roman centurion, seeing how he died, smote his breast and said: “⟦Q 187:5.5⟧This was indeed a righteous man; truly he must have been a Son of God.⟦/Q⟧” From that hour he began to believe in Jesus. Jesus died royally, as he had lived. He went willingly to his ignominious death after providing for the safety of his apostles; he started out bearing his own crossbeam and finished his loving bestowal by handing over his spirit of mortal acquirement to the Paradise Father. After such a life—and at such a death—the Master could truly say, “It is finished.”
ch49.b029: Because it was the preparation day for both the Passover and the Sabbath, the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs of the three men broken so the bodies could be taken down before sundown. Three soldiers came and did so to the two thieves, but to their surprise they found Jesus already dead. To make sure, one of them pierced his left side with a spear. Victims often lingered for two or three days, but the emotional agony and spiritual anguish of Jesus ended his mortal life in a little less than five and one-half hours. About half past three, in the darkness of the sandstorm, David Zebedee sent his last runner to Bethany with the news. John sent the women, in charge of Jude, to the home of Elijah Mark, and himself remained at Golgotha until Joseph and Nicodemus should come for the body. Thus ended a day of tragedy and sorrow for a vast universe, whose myriads of intelligences had shuddered at the crucifixion of their beloved Sovereign.
ch50.title: The Sabbath in the Tomb
ch50.b002: Jesus hung upon the cross for about an hour after his death; he would have been taken down sooner but for the delay in dispatching the two brigands. The rulers of the Jews had planned to have his body thrown into the open burial pits of Gehenna, south of the city, as was the custom with the victims of crucifixion, and there it would have been exposed to the wild beasts. In the meantime Joseph of Arimathea, accompanied by Nicodemus, had gone to Pilate to ask for the body. It was not uncommon for friends of the crucified to offer bribes for such a privilege, and Joseph carried a large sum of money in case it should be needed. But Pilate would not take money for this. When he heard the request, he quickly signed an order authorizing Joseph to take immediate and full possession of the Master’s body. By then the sandstorm had considerably abated, and a group of Jews representing the Sanhedrin had gone out to Golgotha to make sure that Jesus’ body went with those of the brigands to the public pits.
ch50.b003: When Joseph and Nicodemus arrived, they found the soldiers taking Jesus down from the cross and the representatives of the Sanhedrin standing by. Joseph presented Pilate’s order to the centurion, and at once the Jews raised a tumult and sought violently to seize the body. The centurion called four of his soldiers to his side, and with drawn swords they stood astride the Master’s body as it lay on the ground, while the others drove back the angry mob. When order had been restored, the centurion read Pilate’s permit aloud and, stepping aside, said to Joseph: “⟦Q 188:1.1⟧This body is yours to do with as you see fit. I and my soldiers will stand by to see that no man interferes.⟦/Q⟧”
ch50.b005: A crucified person could not be buried in a Jewish cemetery; there was a strict law against it. On the way out to Golgotha, Joseph and Nicodemus had decided to lay Jesus in Joseph’s new family tomb, hewn out of solid rock a short distance north of Golgotha, across the road leading to Samaria. No one had ever lain there, and they thought it fitting that the Master should rest in it. Joseph really believed that Jesus would rise from the dead, but Nicodemus was very doubtful. These two former members of the Sanhedrin had long kept their faith more or less secret, though their fellow councilors had suspected them. From now on they were the most outspoken disciples of Jesus in all Jerusalem.
ch50.b006: At about half past four the little burial procession started across the way. The body, wrapped in a linen sheet, was carried by four men—Joseph, Nicodemus, John, and the Roman centurion—and the faithful women from Galilee followed behind. Inside the tomb, a chamber about ten feet square, they hurriedly prepared the body, for it was the day of preparation and the Sabbath was drawing on apace. Joseph and Nicodemus had brought large quantities of myrrh and aloes, and they wrapped the body with bandages saturated with these solutions. Then they tied a napkin about the face, wrapped the body in a linen sheet, and reverently placed it on a shelf in the tomb. At the centurion’s signal the soldiers helped roll the doorstone up before the entrance. The soldiers then departed for Gehenna with the bodies of the thieves, and the others returned to Jerusalem in sorrow to observe the Passover according to the laws of Moses.
ch50.b007: The women did not go. Since it was not permissible for women to associate with men at such a time, they had hidden near at hand and watched where the Master was laid: Mary Magdalene, Mary the wife of Clopas, Martha another sister of Jesus’ mother, and Rebecca of Sepphoris. They did not think he had been properly prepared for burial. They agreed among themselves to go back to the home of Joseph, rest over the Sabbath, make ready spices and ointments, and return on Sunday morning to prepare the Master’s body properly for the death rest. They lingered by the tomb in the deepening dusk until it was very dark.
ch50.b009: Aside from David Zebedee and Joseph of Arimathea, very few of Jesus’ disciples really believed or understood that he was to arise on the third day. If his followers were unmindful of that promise, his enemies were not. That Friday night, after the Passover supper, about midnight, a group of Jewish leaders gathered at the home of Caiaphas to discuss their fears. Early the next day a committee of Sanhedrists went before Pilate, and their spokesman said: “⟦Q 188:2.2⟧Sir, we remember that this deceiver, Jesus of Nazareth, said, while he was yet alive, ‘After three days I will rise again.’ We have, therefore, come before you to request that you issue such orders as will make the sepulchre secure against his followers, at least until after the third day. We greatly fear lest his disciples come and steal him away by night and then proclaim to the people that he has risen from the dead.⟦/Q⟧”
ch50.b010: Pilate answered: “⟦Q 188:2.3⟧I will give you a guard of ten soldiers. Go your way and make the tomb secure.⟦/Q⟧” They added ten of their own temple guards and marched out to Joseph’s tomb, even on that Sabbath morning. They rolled yet another stone before the entrance and set the seal of Pilate on and around the stones, lest they be disturbed without their knowledge. And these twenty men, ten Jews and ten Romans, remained on watch up to the hour of the resurrection, the Jews carrying them their food and drink.
ch50.b012: Throughout that Sabbath day the apostles and disciples remained in hiding, while all Jerusalem talked of the death on the cross. Almost one and one-half million Jews were in the city, from every part of the Roman Empire and from Mesopotamia. It was the beginning of Passover week, and all these pilgrims would be there to learn of the resurrection and carry the report back to their homes. Just before sunset Mary the mother of Jesus returned with Ruth and Jude to the family at Bethany. David Zebedee stayed at the home of Nicodemus, where his messengers were to assemble early Sunday morning, and the women of Galilee prepared their spices at the home of Joseph of Arimathea. Late Saturday night John Mark summoned the eleven apostles secretly to his father’s house, and just before midnight they gathered in the same upper chamber where they had eaten the Last Supper with their Master two nights before.
ch50.b013: What happened to Jesus during that day and a half, from three o’clock Friday afternoon to three o’clock Sunday morning, is little known. Apparently he died the same natural death as any other mortal in like circumstances. The revelators confess that they do not fully understand his words, “⟦Q 188:3.4⟧Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,⟦/Q⟧” since his Thought Adjuster had long since been personalized. They venture, as their opinion only, that the Creator consciousness of Michael was at large and wholly free; that his former Thought Adjuster was present on earth in command of the assembled celestial hosts; that the spirit identity he had built up in the flesh was consigned to the custody of the Paradise Father; and that his human consciousness slept through those thirty-six hours, so that to him the resurrection of life followed the sleep of death as of the same instant.
ch50.b014: A few correlated facts are recorded. During this time the supreme council of Salvington, numbering one hundred, held an executive meeting on Urantia under the presidency of Gabriel. At least one message passed between Michael and Immanuel on Salvington while the body lay in the tomb, and the Constellation Father of Norlatiadek, who was on Urantia, received instructions from Michael. In the court of the resurrection halls of the first mansion world there now stands the “Michael Memorial,” bearing the inscription: “⟦Q 188:3.11⟧In commemoration of the mortal transit of Jesus of Nazareth on Urantia.⟦/Q⟧” Not all of the personality of Jesus was asleep during this time of apparent death.
ch50.b016: Jesus did not die to atone for the racial guilt of mortal man, nor to appease the wrath of an offended God, nor to ransom man from the fallen princes of the spheres. Sin is not transmitted from parent to child; it is the conscious and deliberate rebellion of an individual will against the Father’s will. Moses taught the dignity and justice of a Creator God, but Jesus portrayed the love and mercy of a heavenly Father. The whole idea of ransom and atonement is incompatible with that Father. “⟦Q 188:5.11⟧There was nothing in the cross which the Father required—only that which Jesus so willingly gave, and which he refused to avoid.⟦/Q⟧”
ch50.b017: Yet the death on the cross has meanings that should not be overlooked; Urantia is known among neighboring worlds as the “World of the Cross.” The great thing is not the fact of his death but “⟦Q 188:4.12⟧the superb manner and the matchless spirit in which he met death.⟦/Q⟧” He made the cross an eternal symbol of the triumph of love over hate when he prayed, “⟦Q 188:5.6⟧Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.⟦/Q⟧” Greater love no man can have than to lay down his life for his friends, but Jesus was willing to lay down his life for his enemies. The cross forever places all relations between God and man upon the family basis: God is the Father; man is his son.
ch50.b018: So, through the long Sabbath night, the twenty watchmen kept guard before the sealed stones of Joseph’s tomb, while within the rock the body wrapped in linen lay still upon its shelf, and the first day of a new week drew near.
ch51.title: The Empty Tomb
ch51.b002: Soon after the burial on Friday afternoon, the chief of the archangels of Nebadon, then present on Urantia, summoned his council of the resurrection to consider how Jesus might be restored. By midnight they had concluded that the creature could do nothing to facilitate the resurrection of the Creator, and they accepted the advice of Gabriel that, since Michael had “⟦Q 189:0.1⟧laid down his life of his own free will, he also had power to take it up again in accordance with his own determination.⟦/Q⟧” Then the Personalized Adjuster of Jesus, in command of the celestial hosts assembled on the planet, spoke to the anxious watchers: “⟦Q 189:0.2⟧Not one of you can do aught to assist your Creator-father in the return to life. As a mortal of the realm he has experienced mortal death; as the Sovereign of a universe he still lives.⟦/Q⟧” From Gabriel down to the most humble cherubim, they all waited in anxious expectancy, gazing on the tomb.
ch51.b003: At two forty-five Sunday morning, seven unidentified Paradise personalities arrived and deployed themselves about the tomb. At ten minutes before three, intense vibrations of commingled material and morontia activities began to issue from Joseph’s new tomb, and at two minutes past three o’clock, this Sunday morning, April 9, A.D. 30, the resurrected morontia form and personality of Jesus of Nazareth came forth from the tomb.
ch51.b004: The body of flesh in which he had lived and wrought for almost thirty-six years still lay in the sepulchre niche, undisturbed and wrapped in the linen sheet, just as Joseph and his companions had left it on Friday. The stone before the entrance had not moved; the seal of Pilate was unbroken; the soldiers were still on guard in the cold darkness. None of them suspected that the body they watched was now a discarded outer covering. Jesus did not come forth as a spirit, nor as Michael of Nebadon in the form he had had before his incarnation. He came forth in the very likeness of the morontia personalities who emerge from the resurrection halls of the first mansion world. No creature had helped him. Appearing beside Gabriel just above the tomb, he greeted him and instructed him to continue in charge of universe affairs. Then, turning to the morontia groups of the seven mansion worlds gathered to welcome their Creator as a creature of their own order, he spoke the first words of his postmortal career: “⟦Q 189:1.10⟧Having finished my life in the flesh, I would tarry here for a short time in transition form that I may more fully know the life of my ascendant creatures and further reveal the will of my Father in Paradise.⟦/Q⟧”
ch51.b006: At ten minutes past three the chief of the archangels approached Gabriel and asked for the mortal body of Jesus. The hosts of heaven, he said, “⟦Q 189:2.1⟧would be spared the memory of enduring the sight of the slow decay of the human form of the Creator and Upholder of a universe.⟦/Q⟧” Permission was granted, and with the aid of the Urantia midwayers they took possession of the body. Unlike the morontia form, this purely material body could not pass out of the sealed sepulchre, and so the secondary midwayers were assigned to roll away the stones. The larger was a huge circular affair, much like a millstone, moving in a groove chiseled out of the rock.
ch51.b007: In the dim light of the morning the watching guards saw this great stone begin to roll away from the entrance, apparently of its own accord. Seized with fear and panic, they fled. The Jews went to their homes and afterward reported to their captain at the temple; the Romans ran to the fortress of Antonia and told the centurion. The Jewish leaders, who had begun the whole sordid business by bribing Judas, now bribed the guards. They paid each of the twenty men and instructed them to say: “⟦Q 189:2.5⟧While we slept during the nighttime, his disciples came upon us and took away the body.⟦/Q⟧”
ch51.b008: The tomb was empty, not because the body had been raised, but because the celestial hosts were permitted to afford it a special dissolution, a return of the “dust to dust” without the delays of time. It underwent the same natural disintegration as every human body, only so accelerated that it became well-nigh instantaneous. The empty tomb was a fact, but it was not the truth of the resurrection. The true evidences are spiritual, corroborated by the many mortals who met, recognized, and communed with the risen Master; before he finally left Urantia, he became a part of the personal experience of almost one thousand human beings. A little after half past four that morning, by the mandate of Michael, Gabriel inaugurated the dispensational resurrection, and the sleeping survivors of the human races since the days of Adam awoke in the resurrection halls of the mansion worlds.
ch51.b010: The ten apostles were asleep in the upper chamber of Elijah Mark’s house, on the very couches where they had reclined at the Last Supper. Thomas had looked them over late Saturday night and gone off alone to Bethpage to grieve. At the house of Joseph of Arimathea the leading women believers had stayed indoors all through the Sabbath, so they knew nothing of the guard, the second stone, or the seal of Pilate. A little before three o’clock, as the first signs of day appeared in the east, five of them set out for the tomb with an abundance of embalming lotions and many linen bandages: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of the Alpheus twins, Salome the mother of the Zebedee brothers, Joanna the wife of Chuza, and Susanna the daughter of Ezra of Alexandria. As they passed out of the Damascus gate they met soldiers fleeing panic-stricken into the city, and they paused for a few minutes before going on. All the way they had said among themselves, “⟦Q 189:4.6⟧Who will help us roll away the stone?⟦/Q⟧”
ch51.b011: About half past three they reached the tomb, which lay in Joseph’s garden on the hillside and faced the east, and found the stone rolled away. They set down their burdens and looked at one another, trembling. Mary Magdalene ventured around the smaller stone and entered. There was just enough dawn to see that the body was gone. In the recess of stone lay only the folded napkin where his head had rested and the bandages, intact, as they had lain before the body was removed; the covering sheet lay at the foot of the niche. Mary uttered a cry of alarm and anguish. The other women, already on edge, were terror-stricken and fled, not stopping until they had run all the way to the Damascus gate. There Joanna, conscience-stricken at having deserted Mary, rallied them, and they started back. The frightened Magdalene rushed up to meet them, exclaiming: “⟦Q 189:4.8⟧He is not there—they have taken him away!⟦/Q⟧”
ch51.b012: All five sat down on the stone near the entrance and talked it over. It had not yet occurred to them that Jesus had risen. They supposed the body had been moved, but then how could the bandages have been left in place, apparently intact, on the burial shelf?
ch51.b014: As they sat there in the gray light, they looked to one side and saw a silent, motionless stranger. Mary Magdalene, thinking he might be the caretaker of the garden, rushed toward him and said, “⟦Q 189:4.10⟧Where have you taken the Master? Where have they laid him? Tell us that we may go and get him.⟦/Q⟧” When he did not answer, she began to weep. Then Jesus spoke: “Whom do you seek?” Mary said: “⟦Q 189:4.10⟧We seek for Jesus who was laid to rest in Joseph’s tomb, but he is gone. Do you know where they have taken him?⟦/Q⟧” Then said Jesus: “⟦Q 189:4.10⟧Did not this Jesus tell you, even in Galilee, that he would die, but that he would rise again?⟦/Q⟧” The words startled them, but the Master was so changed, with his back turned to the dim light, that they did not yet know him. And as they pondered, he addressed the Magdalene with a familiar voice: “Mary.” When she heard that word of well-known sympathy and affectionate greeting, she knew it was the voice of the Master, and she rushed to kneel at his feet, exclaiming, “My Lord, and my Master!” All the others recognized him too and quickly knelt before him.
ch51.b015: As Mary sought to embrace his feet, Jesus said: “⟦Q 189:4.12⟧Touch me not, Mary, for I am not as you knew me in the flesh. In this form will I tarry with you for a season before I ascend to the Father. But go, all of you, now and tell my apostles—and Peter—that I have risen, and that you have talked with me.⟦/Q⟧”
ch51.b017: The women hastened back to the upper chamber and told the ten apostles all that had happened, but the apostles thought they had seen a vision. When Peter heard his own name, however, he rushed out, with John close behind him. As they raced north through the city, Peter’s thoughts alternated between fear and hope; for the first time since the crucifixion he remembered the promise to rise on the third day. In John’s soul a strange ecstasy of joy and hope welled up. John, being younger, arrived first and tarried at the door looking in. Peter rushed up and entered, and saw the empty tomb with the grave cloths so peculiarly arranged; then John went in too. They sat down on the stone to ponder. Peter suggested that enemies had stolen the body and perhaps bribed the guards, but John reasoned that a rifled grave would hardly have been left so orderly. They went back in to examine the cloths more closely.
ch51.b018: When they came out the second time, Mary Magdalene had returned and was weeping before the entrance. The apostles had refused to believe her, and she had longed to come back to the place where she had heard the familiar voice. As she lingered after Peter and John had gone, the Master appeared to her again: “⟦Q 189:5.4⟧Be not doubting; have the courage to believe what you have seen and heard. Go back to my apostles and again tell them that I have risen, that I will appear to them, and that presently I will go before them into Galilee as I promised.⟦/Q⟧” Mary hurried back to the Mark home, but still they would not believe her. Only when Peter and John returned did they cease to ridicule, and then they were filled with fear and apprehension.
ch51.b020: David Zebedee and Joseph of Arimathea heard the women’s report and hurried out to see the tomb. They were the last to view it so, for at half past seven the high priest sent the captain of the temple guards to remove the grave cloths, and he wrapped them in the linen sheet and threw them over a nearby cliff. In the upper chamber most of the apostles were sure the Jews had removed the body. David would not argue. As he left he said: “⟦Q 190:1.3⟧You are the apostles, and you ought to understand these things. I will not contend with you.… I heard the Master say that, after he should die, he would rise on the third day, and I believe him.⟦/Q⟧” On his way out he dropped the bag of Judas, containing all the apostolic funds, in the lap of Matthew Levi.
ch51.b021: By half past nine the last of his twenty-six messengers had arrived at the home of Nicodemus. David assembled them in the courtyard, released them from their oaths, and gave them their last mission: “⟦Q 190:1.5⟧The message which you shall bear to the believers is: ‘Jesus has risen from the dead; the tomb is empty.’⟦/Q⟧” Many tried to dissuade him, but he would not be moved. Shortly before ten o’clock the runners went forth, to Bethany and to every believer center from Beersheba to Damascus and Sidon, from Philadelphia to Alexandria. While the apostles sat in the upper chamber in fear and doubt, these laymen became the first heralds of the risen Savior.
ch51.b023: Shortly after noon, James, the Master’s oldest brother, stood in the garden of Lazarus before the empty tomb of Martha and Mary’s brother, turning over the news David’s messenger had brought. He had long since lost touch with Jesus’ work. Suddenly he became aware of a presence, as if someone had touched him on the shoulder, and turning, he saw a strange form gradually appearing beside him. The form spoke: “⟦Q 190:2.3⟧James, I come to call you to the service of the kingdom. Join earnest hands with your brethren and follow after me.⟦/Q⟧” When James heard his name, he knew it was his eldest brother. He started to fall to his knees, exclaiming, “My father and my brother,” but Jesus bade him stand, and they walked through the garden talking for almost three minutes. Shortly before two o’clock Jesus appeared in the open back door of that same house to his earthly family and their friends, twenty in all: “⟦Q 190:2.6⟧Peace be upon you.… How could you doubt?⟦/Q⟧” As they moved toward him as if to embrace him, he vanished.
ch51.b024: At about a quarter past four he appeared in the midst of some twenty-five women believers at the home of Joseph of Arimathea: “⟦Q 190:3.1⟧Peace be upon you. In the fellowship of the kingdom there shall be neither Jew nor gentile, rich nor poor, free nor bond, man nor woman.⟦/Q⟧” About half past four, behind securely fastened doors at the home of one Flavius, he appeared to some forty Greek believers: “⟦Q 190:4.1⟧In the kingdom of my Father there shall be neither Jew nor gentile; you will all be brethren—the sons of God.⟦/Q⟧” By evening the rumors had reached the rulers. Caiaphas convened the Sanhedrin at eight o’clock, and they voted to throw out of the synagogues anyone who spoke of the resurrection, but the meeting broke up in confusion bordering on panic. They had thought they were through with Jesus; their real trouble with the man of Nazareth had just begun.
ch51.b026: A few minutes before five that afternoon, about three miles out of Jerusalem, two shepherd brothers from Emmaus, Cleopas and Jacob, were trudging homeward, arguing about the rumors of the empty tomb. Cleopas was half a mind to believe; Jacob insisted it was probably a fraud. A traveler came alongside them. Cleopas had heard Jesus teach and had eaten with him several times, but he did not recognize him. When the stranger asked what they were discussing, Cleopas told him of Jesus of Nazareth, “⟦Q 190:5.3⟧a prophet mighty in word and in deed before God and all the people,⟦/Q⟧” of the crucifixion, and of the women who said they had found the tomb empty and talked with him. Jacob broke in: “⟦Q 190:5.3⟧but they did not see Jesus.⟦/Q⟧”
ch51.b027: Jesus said to them: “⟦Q 190:5.4⟧How slow you are to comprehend the truth!⟦/Q⟧” As they walked, he reminded them that this Jesus had always taught that his kingdom was not of this world and had foretold that he would be put to death and arise on the third day, and he opened the Scriptures: that such a Deliverer “⟦Q 190:5.4⟧shall be as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land,⟦/Q⟧” that he would “bind up the brokenhearted,” that “⟦Q 190:5.4⟧all who sit in darkness shall see the great light of eternal salvation.⟦/Q⟧” Not a word did the brothers speak all the way. At their humble dwelling they constrained him to stay, for it was near nightfall. At table they gave him the bread to bless, and as he began to break it and hand it to them, their eyes were opened. When Cleopas said, “It is the Master —,” he vanished. “⟦Q 190:5.6⟧No wonder our hearts burned within us as he spoke to us while we walked along the road!⟦/Q⟧” They would not stop to eat. They hurried back through the dark to Jerusalem, and about nine o’clock that evening they broke in upon the apostles in the upper chamber, declaring that they had seen Jesus and talked with him.
